table.text: To determine sample size requirements, we conducted an a-priori power analysis, using G*Power 3.0.10 (Faul et al., 2007). To achieve a power of 0.80 at α = 0.05, assuming a mediumsmall effect size (f = .10), the suggested sample size was 145 participants. As we wished to draw data from a representative sample of Dutch residents with regard to gender, age, province, and education level (see https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd section 2.1), we settled for a sample of 400 people.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Our participants' age varied between 18 and 85 (M = 50.92, SD = 16.95).
Participants completed a 45-minute online Qualtrics (https://www.qualtrics.com/) survey in Dutch.

After each text, participants completed the following measures: Manipulation check of state of change (single-item); self-reported threat and challenge; threat and challenge appraisal (i.e., personal relevance, demands, resources).
Participants were presented with a text describing the status quo, followed by a text describing the social change.
Participants were asked how often they engage with LGBTQ+ issues and sustainability, on a scale from 1 ("Never") to 5 ("Daily").
Participants were asked how responsible they felt toward LGBTQ+ issues and sustainability, on a scale from 1 ("Not at all") to 5 ("Very much").

info.title: THE TRANSFORMATIVE SIDE OF SOCIETAL STRESS

text.text: Research showed that social changes elicit threat, which is considered a negative response to be avoided to improve intergroup relations.
However, this approach overlooks the transformative potential of positive stress (challenge) for progressive social changes.
To address this gap, we investigated whether, and if so, under what conditions, social change is perceived as threatening or challenging.
Results from a representative Dutch sample (N = 411) revealed that social change is more threatening than the status quo.

Furthermore, the instrumental (vs. symbolic) aspects of change, and its perceived demands and uncertainty heighten threat, while the ingroup and system (vs. personal) dimensions of change, and social resources and support buffer against threat.
Our results offer insight into what factors promote more adaptive (challenge) rather than maladaptive (threat) responses to social changes.
They encourage a critical perspective on social change, framing threat not as inherently negative but as tensions to be navigated.

In 2020, following years of advocacy and protests, the Dutch government proposed an amendment to the Gender Recognition Act to simplify the process for legally changing one's gender (Tweede Kamer der Staten-Generaal, 2020).

text.text: Despite wide support from the Dutch
LGBTQ+ community, the proposed changes faced substantial backlash and ultimately did not pass (Slevin, 2022).

text.text: To this day, grassroots organizations continue to struggle for improved healthcare for transgender people, showcasing their ongoing commitment toward trans rights (Westerink, 2024).

text.text: This illustrates that, while social change 1 is crucial for addressing systemic inequalities, advancing minority liberation often involves overcoming entrenched opposition and sustaining efforts despite setbacks, underscoring the importance of understanding stress and coping associated with social change.
In social psychology, it is well documented that social changes can trigger negative stress ('threat') and hostility (Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018; Scheepers & Knight, 2020).
text.formatted: In social psychology, it is well documented that social changes can trigger negative stress ('threat') and hostility <ref type="bibr">(Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Scheepers & Knight, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, this field of study maintains a narrow perspective on how to address the stress of social change, mostly emphasizing threat avoidance strategies, while disregarding the transformative power of more positive stress ('challenge').
This might stem from previous work somewhat overlooking the complex range of psychological and societal factors that render change stressful.

This paper addresses these limitations by providing a more comprehensive, and critical perspective on stress and coping with hierarchy-disruptive social change (vs. status quo), where with hierarchy-disruptive social change we mean material and systemic social change that aims to dismantle unjust hierarchies, and that is rooted in minoritized communities' 1 Social change refers to systemic transformations that shift power, influencing cultural norms, group dynamics, and societal institutions.
This concept is well-established in social psychology, and this paper specifically explores progressive changes designed to improve the status of minorities.
objectives and social movements initiatives.
To achieve this, we investigated the role that personal relevance, demands, and resources appraisals play in eliciting either threat or challenge.
Beyond such basic processes, we also addressed three levels on which such changes have an impact (personal, ingroup, system), and two facets of change (instrumental vs. symbolic).

Finally, we explored the differential effects of several types of appraisal (personal vs. social demands and resources, uncertainty, support) on experiencing social change as a challenge or as a threat.

Social changes have been associated with a loss of normative and structural integrity in society (de la Sablonnière, 2017), often leading to threat, uncertainty and anxiety (Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018).
text.formatted: Social changes have been associated with a loss of normative and structural integrity in society (de la Sablonnière, 2017), often leading to threat, uncertainty and anxiety <ref type="bibr">(Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this perspective, Scheepers (2009) demonstrated that when a rigid hierarchy becomes unstable in a minimal group scenario, high-status members, in particular, felt psychophysiologically threatened by the potential loss of their privileged position. text.text: Threat of social change was also observed among White American individuals interacting with a high-SES Latino confederate (Mendes et al., 2007), and in Dutch men discussing progressive gender roles with women (Scheepers et al., 2009), specifically in the form of cardiovascular responses.
text.formatted: Threat of social change was also observed among White American individuals interacting with a high-SES Latino confederate <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Mendes et al., 2007)</ref>, and in Dutch men discussing progressive gender roles with women <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Scheepers et al., 2009)</ref>, specifically in the form of cardiovascular responses.

text.text: In the first study, heightened threat was linked to more negative treatment and avoidance of the confederate; in the second, it was associated with potentially suppressed sexism, suggesting men may conceal it when threatened in intergroup interactions.

Taken together, these findings illustrate that social changes are often threatening, especially for dominant group members, and may have negative effects on their attitudes toward oppressed communities and progressive initiatives.

This has primarily led to recommendations for avoiding such threat responses, employing strategies such as dualidentity formation, or scripted interactions (Avery et al., 2009; Scheepers et al., 2014).

text.text: Such an approach underscores a broader tendency within psychology to prioritize societal harmony and the absence of conflict as ideal states, while mainly considering negative emotions such as anxiety as undesirable (see Wright & Baray, 2012).
text.formatted: Such an approach underscores a broader tendency within psychology to prioritize societal harmony and the absence of conflict as ideal states, while mainly considering negative emotions such as anxiety as undesirable (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Wright & Baray, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: However, such efforts aim to reduce symptomatic discomfort and thereby risk maintaining the status quo rather than address the range of psychological and structural factors underlying responses to change.
A more critical view of stress and coping with social change highlights the constructive role of conflict and negative affect in driving progress.

According to critical theory (Marx & Engels, 1848; Bohrer, 2019), through the clash of opposing forces (i.e., oppression and resistance), exploitative power structures are problematized, opening the possibility of more equitable and just social relations.
text.formatted: According to critical theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Marx & Engels, 1848;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bohrer, 2019)</ref>, through the clash of opposing forces (i.e., oppression and resistance), exploitative power structures are problematized, opening the possibility of more equitable and just social relations.

text.text: As a result, threat may be an unavoidable feature of successful progressive social changes.
Within this perspective, approach-based coping, rather than avoidance-based coping, with the stress of social change could represent a transformative opportunity, accompanied by challenge.

In fact, exposure to stressful events can also enhance resilience and well-being, as individuals who experienced and actively coped with adversity report better functionality than those who did not at all (Rutter, 2012).
text.formatted: In fact, exposure to stressful events can also enhance resilience and well-being, as individuals who experienced and actively coped with adversity report better functionality than those who did not at all <ref type="bibr">(Rutter, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, while challenge remains a taxing, sometimes aversive, experience, it may nonetheless serve as a catalyst for adaptive functioning and growth when approached constructively.
However, limited empirical evidence has been accumulated on how people cope with hierarchy-disruptive social changes, compared to individual life events and encounters.

As a result, central to the current paper's approach is appreciating the existence of both maladaptive (threat) and adaptive (challenge) forms of stress of systemic and progressive social change, manifesting in the general population.
Stress responses have been examined using physiological measures based on the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT).
This model was first introduced by Blascovich and Tomaka (1996) to explain cardiovascular reactivity and performance during stressful situations.
text.formatted: This model was first introduced by <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Blascovich and Tomaka (1996)</ref> to explain cardiovascular reactivity and performance during stressful situations.

text.text: According to the BPS-CT, whenever an individual engages in a motivated performance task, they may enter a state of negative stress (threat) or positive stress (challenge).
A sense of engagement with the task is a prerequisite of threat and challenge, which for the case of social change can be conceptualized as the personal relevance of the issue at hand.
Threat negatively affects performance, as well as health outcomes and psychological well-being, whereas challenge positively relates to these indicators.

More specifically, while both states may bring about negative emotions (e.g., anger for challenge, fear for threat), and increased reactivity of both the body (i.e., increased cardiovascular responses) and mind (i.e. cognitive engagement), only threat is considered a maladaptive response (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010).
text.formatted: More specifically, while both states may bring about negative emotions (e.g., anger for challenge, fear for threat), and increased reactivity of both the body (i.e., increased cardiovascular responses) and mind (i.e. cognitive engagement), only threat is considered a maladaptive response <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Applying the BPS-CT to social change thus has the potential of acknowledging a fuller spectrum of stress-related outcomes, some of which may be constructive for progressive goals.
Given the novel application of BPS-CT to hierarchy-disruptive social change, we used a self-report approach to conceptually validate this extension.
While physiological measures are central to traditional BPS-CT research, they are impractical for large samples and offer limited insight into subjective appraisals.
Our scale captures psychological evaluations of threat and challenge in response to social change.
The perception of threat or challenge depends on whether the individual's resources are deemed sufficient to meet the demands of the situation.

In the context of social change, individuals navigate shifts in cultural norms, power struggles against the oppression of marginalized groups, and sociopolitical 'performances', for instance when voicing one's opinion during a discussion, or participating in protests.

These dynamics can lead to various existential and epistemic stressors, like uncertainties and exposure to psychological and physical violence (Cropley & Jost, 2024; de la Sablonnière, 2017), encompassing possible demands of social change.
text.formatted: These dynamics can lead to various existential and epistemic stressors, like uncertainties and exposure to psychological and physical violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cropley & Jost, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">de la Sablonnière, 2017)</ref>, encompassing possible demands of social change.

text.text: Uncertainty in particular may play a crucial role in shaping perceptions of threat during social change, as individuals often face unprecedented circumstances.
To effectively manage these demands, factors such as support networks, and personal resilience play a critical role, encompassing forms of resources.
Given the novelty, severity, and systemic character of social change, individuals are less likely to have immediate access to the resources needed to effectively cope with these exacerbated demands.
In fact, relevant knowledge and abilities are considered vital resources to cope with demands, as well as social support, and personal disposition (Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996).

text.text: Yet, the assumed availability of such resources may be unrealistic when faced with the unprecedented nature of many hierarchy-disruptive social changes.
As a result, we hypothesized that hierarchy-dispersive social changes would elicit a stronger self-reported threat response compared to the existing status quo within a society.

We further hypothesized that the relationship between social change and self-reported threat and challenge would be moderated by perceived personal relevance 2 , and mediated by perceived demands and resources.

Finally, we explored the specific effect of uncertainty on threat and challenge, given its pivotal role during social changes.
According to Power Basis Theory (Pratto & Stewart, 2020), power struggles between dominant and minoritized groups are embedded in multi-level systems shaped by history, politics, and culture.

text.text: Social change is therefore not self-contained but impacts institutions and affects personal, group, and systemic levels (de la Sablonnière, 2017).

That is, whereas personal-level change can be seen in shifts in individual well-being and the adoption of new behaviors, ingroup-level effects are observable in the shifts in status and relations among social groups and socioeconomic classes in society, such as achieving more equitable rights, or dynamics of discrimination and resistance.

Finally, systemic effects are observable in the dismantlement, reform, or introduction of legislations, institutions, and norms, such as transitioning from insurance-based healthcare to universal healthcare.

Personal, (in)group, and systemic effects of social changes thus all manifest in individuals' psychological responses, influencing stress levels and shaping the cognitive appraisal of threat and challenge.
In this context, the way individuals perceive and respond to these changes is significantly affected by the resources available to them.

When individuals recognize the psychological and material support that their communities can offer, they may feel better equipped to handle the demands of social change, rather than relying solely on their potentially more limited personal resources.
This highlights the importance of considering not just personal demands and resources, but also broader social resources, when studying the impact of social changes.
Previous research on social change has focused mainly on individual interactions or personal effects of systemic shifts like economic instability.
This study examined threat and challenge responses across personal, ingroup, and system levels, and their interaction with both individual and social appraisals of demands and support resources.

Following de la Sablonnière's (2017) topological work, the loss of normative and institutional structures typical of social changes threatens the cultural identity of all community members, as well as their material conditions, and moral foundations.
This suggests that social change elicits different threats and challenges to be categorized in symbolic and instrumental facets (see intergroup-threat theory; Rios et al., 2018).

text.text: Shifts in cultural identities, values, and beliefs represent symbolic threat or challenge.

For example, the failed Dutch proposal to let people change their gender without the need of a medical diagnosis (Slevin, 2022) could have potentially brought about new gender practices and concepts for both trans and cis people in the Netherlands, as it would introduce a new definition of gender and a sense of fluidity and uncertainty around gender identity.

For example, the advocated increase in minimum wage by a Dutch labor union (Hanse, 2022), would have impacted people's personal financial resources (e.g., increase purchasing power), as well as the Dutch market (e.g., increase inflation if business owners' pass labor costs to consumers).

text.text: However, there remains a scarcity of empirical evidence to support these theoretical insights.

To address this empirical gap, this study explored which facets of change may elicit threat and challenge, distinguishing between instrumental (power, material resources, safety, health) and symbolic (morality, identity, meaning, status).
In the current research we investigated whether progressive social changes elicit a selfreported threat or challenge response among people from a representative sample of the Netherlands.
To develop a comprehensive and critical account on what contributes to challenge and threat during hierarchy-disruptive social change we investigated three main classes of determinants.

First of all, we examine proximal psychological appraisal factors, such as the perceived personal relevance of the topic of change as well as the demands of social change, and the perceived resources to cope with these demands.

Our hypotheses were: (1) compared to the status quo, people will perceive social changes to be more threatening; (2) social changes will elicit a stronger response the more participants find social change to be self-relevant (moderation); social changes will elicit a stronger threat response the more participants find social change to be demanding, and to overpower the resources available to them (mediation).

Second, we explored more distal factors which might in turn influence these appraisals, namely (1) the level where change has its impact (personal, ingroup, system), (2) the facets of this change, in terms of instrumental (rights, material resources, safety, health) or symbolic (identity, morality, meaning, status) changes, and (3) the type of appraisal (i.e., personal vs. social demands and resources, uncertainty, and support).
Finally, we modeled our social change manipulation on two real-world issues, food degrowth and trans rights, using a within-subjects design to reflect how change occurs.
Our goal was not to directly compare these topics, but to test the generalizability of our perspective, so we selected timely, socially relevant yet distinct issues.
Though not our main aim, we also explore how different contexts elicit varied stress appraisals.
Doing so, we balanced conceptual insight with contextual sensitivity, answering calls for theory grounded in real-world complexity (Pratto & Stewart, 2020).

text.text: First, after providing informed consent, participants indicated their familiarity, sense of responsibility, and attitudes toward sustainability and LGBTQ+ people.
Afterwards, participants read four short pieces of text, which represented our manipulation of topic and state of change.

After each text, participants completed the following measures: Manipulation check of state of change (single-item); self-reported threat and challenge; threat and challenge appraisal (i.e., personal relevance, demands, resources).
The survey closed with some demographic questions: political orientation, age, assigned sex at birth, gender identity, sexual orientation, ethnicity, subjective socio-economic status.

text.text: Unless otherwise indicated, all questionnaires employed a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 ("Not at all") to 7 ("Very much") to measure agreement with the given statements.
Participants were presented with a text describing the status quo, followed by a text describing the social change.
Instability, disruption, and novelty are considered main characteristics of social change (de la Sablonnière, 2017).

Thus, in the status quo condition, we described the situation as stable and structured ("[…] is a pillar of Dutch […] measures."), and long-standing ("This will remain much the same for a long time to come.").

In the social change condition, we introduced an unprecedented social change ("It is very likely that changes will take place in the Netherlands in the near future […] with the introduction of various measures […]"), and an unstable disruption of the social and normative structure of Dutch society ("These changes are expected to have a significant impact on the country in general, and people's daily lives.").
For the food degrowth condition, the status quo focused on renewable energy production, which is well-established in the Netherlands.
The social change text introduced the possibility of reducing food waste in the Netherlands by regulating more strictly food production and import.

For the trans right condition, the status quo condition focused on samesex marriage; the social change text introduced the possibility of becoming more inclusive by removing binary-gender indicators in official documents.
Tailoring the content to the participants, the texts emphasized activities common to any Dutch citizen, such as "doing groceries", and "renewing documents".
To further increase a sense of relevance of the social chance scenario, we stressed the vast impact that social change may have ("This will eventually affect […] everyone in the Netherlands.").
All texts were less than 100 words long, to limit cognitive load.
The two scenarios were selected as illustrative cases of social change, rather than as subjects of direct comparison.
Manipulation Check.

We evaluated the effectiveness of the manipulation of state of social change by asking participant to rate whether the text they read suggested that drastic changes were about to happen in the Netherlands.
This was done for both the status quo condition and the social change condition.
We used a 48-item self-report scale to measure threat and challenge, based on the biopsychosocial model (Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996).

text.text: This study investigated stress and coping responses to progressive social changes, examining their effects on self-reported threat and challenge in a representative Dutch sample across two social change topics.
It further investigated how personal relevance, demands, and resources influenced these responses.

Additionally, it explored differential effects on stress responses across personal, ingroup, and system levels of change; instrumental and symbolic facets of change; personal vs. social demands and resources, uncertainty, support types of appraisal.
In line with our hypothesis, we found that social change related to food degrowth was viewed as more threatening compared to maintaining the status quo.
However, social change related to trans rights was perceived as more of a challenge instead.
Personal relevance moderated the relationship between social change and threat and challenge, so that higher personal relevance amplified perception of stress in either direction.
Moreover, how individuals appraise demands and resources mediated the relationship between social change and threat and challenge.
These results are generally in line with the appraisal part of the BPS-CT.
Exploratory analyses showed that the impact of change at a personal level elicited more threat than the impact on the ingroup and system levels.
Instrumental facets of change elicited more threat than symbolic facets.
Finally, uncertainty appraisal played a prominent role in eliciting threat, while social resources and support appraisal help mitigating it, and more so than more personal factors.
Our results suggest that social change generally elicited stronger perceptions of stress compared with maintaining the status quo.
Social change was also perceived as more personally relevant and drastic than maintaining the status quo.

Furthermore, consistent with BPS-CT predictions, social change heightened perceptions of demands and reduced perceptions of available resources compared with the status quo, and such demands and resources mediated the relationship between social change and threat and challenge.

Previous research already provided extensive evidence on the threat responses individuals experience to shifting norms and relations between social groups (Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018; Scheepers & Knight, 2020).

text.text: However, such work primarily focused on negative aspects of changes, such as the loss of status among dominant group members, and on intergroups rather than hierarchydisruptive social change.

Our findings extend this work by applying the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; Blascovich & Mendes, 2000; Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996) to more ecologically valid, systemic, and consequential forms of social change.

text.text: Compared with previous work (Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018; 2019), our findings add nuance to how people may respond to social change by suggesting that whether change is appraised as threatening or challenging depends on a more complex interplay of situational and personal factors that previously considered, including its perceived self-relevance and drasticness, and the actual extent to which the demands associated with change are actually perceived to outweigh available resources.

text.text: In the present study, participants perceived social change related to food degrowth as highly drastic and personally relevant, as well as more demanding than the resources they perceived as available, thus, ultimately threatening.

In contrast, changing gender markers in official documents, which we expected to be highly threatening given the identity and safety threats associated with trans identities and rights (Morgenroth & Ryan, 2021), was perceived as moderately drastic and only weakly personally relevant, with perceived resources outweighing demands, and was therefore ultimately appraised as challenging.

This may suggest that social change as particularly threatening when it entails broader material and systemic disruption, rather than changes that primarily alter recognition or inclusion within existing institutional arrangements.

Additionally, while previous work has often paired opposition with threat (Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018), our findings suggest that the broader population, tentatively including those who support or benefit from progressive changes, may experience some degree of threat.

These findings have important ramifications.
First, stress is closely tied to poor health outcomes, with maladaptive coping mechanisms exacerbating these effects.

Societal changes, like economic crises, heighten chronic stress (Kopp et al., 2007), and can lead to depression, diminished well-being and vitality, and poorer physical health (McLoughlin et al., 2023).

text.text: Second, stress influences behavioral responses that may be critical for fostering progressive change itself.

Engaging with social change initiatives, such as activism among transgender protestors, can elevate psychological distress, with detrimental effects on collective action intentions (Breslow et al., 2015).

text.text: However, recognizing that stress can be framed as a challenge rather than only as a threat opens the door to a healthier and more constructive view of stress in the context of social change.

Finally, rather than mapping onto simple gains and losses or support and opposition, threat and challenge in response to social change may depend on a more complex interplay of factors, including the extent to which change is perceived to jeopardize existing hierarchies and institutions and how personally relevant it is, and, more importantly, how the situational
Consistent with the BPS-CT, our findings suggest that personal relevance heightens stress responses, as it moderates the relationship between social change and threat and challenge.
Furthermore, individuals viewed social change as more demanding compared to the status quo and felt less resourceful to handle these demands.
In turn, higher perceived demands were associated with stronger threat, and higher perceived resources buffered against these threats.

text.text: Collectively, these shifting scenarios can impose negative stress on the general population, potentially overshadowing the benefits of progressive social change.
These demands manifest in two broad classes of outcomes: health and behavior.
On the one hand, the demands induced by social change can negatively affect mental and physical health, contributing to issues such as anxiety, depression, or even stress-related illnesses.
On the other hand, these demands can also influence behavior, motivating actions such as lowered civic engagement and activism, or withdrawal, and resistance against change.
Understanding these dual impacts is crucial for addressing the unintended consequences of the demands of progressive social change.
Consistent with this theoretical corpus, we found that uncertainty was the strongest predictor of threat of social change, even when accounting for more tangible demands.
According to Hogg (2000), uncertainty reduction is a key motivator in clarifying personal and social identities.

text.text: This drive becomes especially significant during societal upheavals when the lack of clear norms fosters uncertainty.
Such societal uncertainty may lead to ineffective coping mechanisms.

For instance, uncertainty, defined as the perception that society lacks clear norms, such as during the dissolution of feudalism, was linked to individuals turning to materialism for fulfillment (Chang & Arkin, 2002), resulting in life dissatisfaction and increased anxiety.

text.text: Moreover, members of dominant groups may strive to maintain the status quo as a means of preserving their relative sense of certainty (Hogg, 2000).

text.text: This further underscores the importance of addressing feelings of uncertainty and demands more generally, as these can impact individuals' willingness to engage with, and adapt to, progressive social changes.
Resources for Social Change.

Following the BPS-CT, to handle the demands of social change, individuals may be able to draw various resources, such as personal attributes, social support networks, and institutional assistance (Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996).

text.text: Psychological resilience, defined as the capacity to bounce back from adversity, is often bolstered by resources such as skills and networks, emphasizing their role in mitigating threats during social changes (Ungar, 2021).
Additionally, social support, for instance, is a critical resource that can reduce fear and stress by fostering a sense of security and belonging (Hornstein & Eisenberger, 2017).
text.formatted: Additionally, social support, for instance, is a critical resource that can reduce fear and stress by fostering a sense of security and belonging <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hornstein & Eisenberger, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these represent examples of resources that can be used to navigate the threat of social change.
However, drastic social changes often disrupt access to resources due to its unpredictable and destabilizing nature.
For example, social changes may challenge personal identity and social roles, making it harder for individuals to leverage social networks effectively.

Crucially, our study centers on hierarchy-disruptive social changes (i.e., Food degrowth policies and expanded trans rights through gender-inclusive document reforms, both nationlevel initiatives), and so addresses a critical gap in social psychology: Prejudice and inequalities are often investigated from the narrower perspective of interpersonal relations, such as the interaction between dominant and marginalized group members (Pratto & Stewart, 2020).

text.text: By concentrating solely on individual biases, we risk missing the structural forces at play (e.g., institutionalized discrimination, or economic systems reinforcing inequality), and, consequently, more systemic solutions necessary to drive progressive social changes.
Our exploratory analyses indicated that participants often perceive a greater threat at the personal level compared to when considering the ingroup or systemic levels.

This somewhat contradicts cognitive appraisal theory (see Ellsworth, 1991), according to which individuals who focus on their personal circumstances may be more accurate and thus able to restore a greater sense of control.

text.text: Concurrently, we observed that the primary buffers against the threat of social change were social resources and support, whereas both personal demands and personal resources had a smaller effect on threat and challenge responses.
These observations together suggest that communities and institutions play an important role in social changes, beyond just individuallevel factors.

Although the concept of collective resource mobilization is not new to the sociological literature of social movements (Jenkins, 1983; McCarthy & Zald, 1977), this is an initial attempt to bring this level of analysis to the study of a BPS-CT of social change.

text.text: Resource mobilization theorists argue that grievances (e.g., injustice, losses) play a secondary role compared to the availability of resources in determining whether social movements, and their members, can sustain collective efforts toward progress.
These resources may be instrumental, based on power, or mobilizing in nature.
In line with this perspective, our findings suggest that collective resources may provide an effective way for individuals to cope with the very grievances brought about by social changes.
So that dealing with social change may come down to managing the tension between, on the one hand, individualized risks and uncertainties, and on the other hand, collective resilience and resources.
Our results showed that instrumental facets of change (e.g., economic losses) were perceived as more intensely threatening than symbolic ones (e.g., threats to cultural norms).
Consistent with our findings, research on the impact of the COVID-pandemic suggested that realistic threat more consistently predicts anxiety than symbolic threat (Kachanoff et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Consistent with our findings, research on the impact of the COVID-pandemic suggested that realistic threat more consistently predicts anxiety than symbolic threat <ref type="bibr">(Kachanoff et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This result might further explain why changes related to food degrowth, which more directly impacts resources and economic stability, were perceived as more threatening than changes related to trans rights, which primarily involve shifts in gender values and identity.
This is particularly relevant for the Netherlands.

In light of the Dutch farmers protests and material uncertainties deriving from the invasion of Ukraine-both happening around the time of data collection, material changes might have felt more threatening to Dutch residents than symbolic ones.
The Dutch emphasis on individualism and privacy may further explain why changes to gender markers in personal documents felt less personally relevant, and thus less demanding or threatening.
This likely contributed to the challenge responses observed.
In contrast, more public or material changes, like access to gender-affirming healthcare, might have elicited stronger threat reactions.

Globally, such policies often provoke significant resistance, as seen in recent U.S. legislation by Republican lawmakers targeting gender-affirming care, public spaces, and trans participation in sports.

While speculative, these interpretations highlight the need to consider historical and geopolitical context in studying social change, often neglected in social psychology's preference for abstract, decontextualized scenarios.
Our choice of a concrete, locally grounded case reflects this concern and resists overgeneralizing Western-centric responses.

Rather than an incidental obstacle, threat may be a recurrent aspect of social change to the extent that such change is systemic, disruptive to existing hierarchies and institutions, personally relevant, and perceived as entailing demands that exceed the resources available to individuals.

Based on these observations, we argue that threat is not inherently negative and to be avoided or necessarily downregulated, but rather one that individuals and movements may benefit from learning how to navigate in order to transform threat into challenge.
From a critical theory perspective, such stress is intrinsic to transformation, as struggles for minority liberation involve tension and resistance.

While reducing threat responses may seem ideal, avoiding them can mean ignoring inequality or disengaging from the risks and responsibilities of change, ultimately reinforcing the status quo by leaving root injustices unaddressed.

For example, as the LGBTQ+ Pride movement grew in the 1970s, the mainstream agenda, largely led by white gay men, began to narrow its focus to sexual orientation (e.g., marriage equality), while excluding original demands around race and sex worker's rights.
This was often accompanied by fearing that supposedly broader, more controversial demands would jeopardize the struggle's credibility and efficacy (Gorman, 2019).
text.formatted: This was often accompanied by fearing that supposedly broader, more controversial demands would jeopardize the struggle's credibility and efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gorman, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: By not addressing such uncertainties and risks, the movement missed the opportunity to foster a truly intersectional vision of solidarity, ultimately leaving trans people and people of color feeling marginalized and forced to leave and organize their own separate spaces.

Rather than avoidance, we propose that approach-based coping (challenge) with the stress of social change could better promote outcomes beneficial to progressive social change itself, such as psychological wellbeing, critical awareness, and collective action intentions.

For example, in the context of pro-environmental social change, an approach-oriented (challenge) coping mechanism was shown to link stress responses to increased collective action intentions despite the underlying existential threat appraisal (Stollberg & Jonas, 2021).

text.text: Our multilevel approach revealed that social resources significantly buffer the threat of social change.

This highlights the need to critically reassess the overemphasis on individual responsibility in sustaining progress, common in sustainability discourse, where calls to reduce personal carbon footprints often ignore systemic barriers and collective solutions like degrowth or alternatives to capitalist consumption.
In a context of neoliberal individualism, this focus on self-reliance overlooks the vital role of collective support.
We argue that progressive change requires community-led efforts, including political education, direct action, and mental health support.
Despite our study made an initial contribution to a finer grained understanding of stress response to social change, there are limitations to take into account when interpreting our results.
First, the proponents of the BPS-CT caution against the reliance on self-reported measures of threat and challenge.
Beyond issues of social desirability, stress responses are often too salient for people to fully grasp before coping emerges.

Although we mitigated this concern by providing clear definitions and instructions on the nature of the response we were seeking, in our current line of work we investigate this mechanism employing more covert measures, namely cardiovascular indicators of threat and challenge.

At the same time, the use of selfreported measures allowed us to gather initial evidence from a broader and more representative sample, while lab studies usually imply limiting samples to around 100 participants, as well as relying on student participants.
Nonetheless, our sample underrepresented several minoritized groups in the Netherlands, especially people of color and sexual minorities.

Future studies should strive for greater inclusivity rather than representativeness, as this would shed light on how threat and challenge responses vary among minoritized groups who are often the most affected by and the most involved in progressive social changes.

To further examine how demands and resources shape responses to social change, future research should consider utilizing verbal explanations, or more refined scales to identify specific demands and resources that individuals rely on, and possibly start classifying them in relevant categories, such as skills, moral resources, and so on.
Such insights could reveal which particular demands and resources more specifically impact responses to different social changes.
In connection to our findings on the importance of social resources, future studies could explore who provides these resources and how they are mobilized within communities.
For instance, investigating the roles of social movements, peer networks, or institutional support systems could help clarify the mechanisms through which individuals access social resources.
Furthermore, future research could experimentally manipulate whether individuals navigate these changes on a personal level, together with their communities, or integrated with the broader system.

This deeper understanding could reveal strategies for improving access to essential resources, even in the face of unprecedented social changes, and highlight ways to strengthen collective resilience.

Ultimately, social change forces individuals to dynamically manage their personal demands, such as coping with uncertainty, alongside their access to resources, particularly collective ones like social support and community resilience.

This dynamic balance determines whether people experience such changes as a threat or challenge, which in turn we theoretically speculate has implications for individual well-being and physical health, and sociopolitical behavioral responses: Those perceiving progressive social change as a threat may experience increased anxiety, and disengagement; those perceiving it as a challenge may experience positive growth, and motivation to participate in collective action.

Minoritized communities in Western societies continue to grapple with systemic exploitation and inequalities, and as progressive social changes unfold, these can often feel threatening to the general population.
While this sense of threat is not inherently negative, it is crucial to understand and promote healthier coping strategies such as approach-based (challenge) ones.

These insights are important not just for individuals navigating evolving norms and institutions, but potentially also for social movements, which frequently encounter backlash, and failures, and need to continue organizing and mobilizing despite setbacks.

Given that progressive changes take conflict, and effort to establish and maintain, unhealthy coping mechanisms can drive those needing to adapt to or advocating for these changes into a state of paralysis, ultimately perpetuating the status quo.
